title: Ang 1352: Jaijavanti
hookLine: Guru Tegh Bahadur's four hymns in the last raga
tomorrow: after the last raga, verses in a style older than the Gurus. why?

lines: THE RAGA, OR A TUNE FOR ALL?
cards: A song stuck in your head came with a tune you didn't pick. Change the tune and the same words land differently.
Jaijavanti is the last raga in the Granth, and on ang 1352 it holds four hymns of Guru Tegh Bahadur, the ninth Guru. That answers yesterday's question.
It also opens an argument Sikh musicians still have: should these words be sung in the raga the Guru named, or in a tune anyone can sing?

teach.b: First, the hymns. They're short and urgent. In paraphrase, one says: remember the Lord, remember; that's your real work.
Another asks the mind: what will become of you? A third sounds like a clock: it's passing, it's passing, this life is slipping by. The fourth says: take shelter in the Name.
Now the two views, each at its best. Some ragis and kirtan teachers hold to the raga.

teach.h: ONE VIEW: THE HEADING IS THE GURU'S.
teach.b: Every hymn in the Granth carries a raga in its heading, and they hear that heading as part of the hymn.

teach.h: OTHER VIEW: A TUNE THE ROOM CAN SING.
teach.b: Jaijavanti's mood was chosen for these words; sing them in another tune and something the Guru gave goes missing. Their case: the heading is in the Guru's book, so it isn't decoration.
Other Sikhs sing Gurbani in simpler tunes a whole hall can join. Their case: the Gurus sang among ordinary people, and a hymn everyone can sing reaches hearts a trained-only raga might miss.
Both sides love the same words. One points to the heading; the other points to the sangat singing together. Nobody has to win today.
Listen for what each side protects.
One guards the Guru's chosen mood. The other guards the room's voice.

how: Ragis sing Guru Tegh Bahadur's Jaijavanti hymns in kirtan; some keep strictly to the raga named in the heading, while other kirtan uses simpler tunes so the whole sangat can sing along.

s: Jaijavanti holds hymns from many Gurus
on ang 1352 it holds four hymns of Guru Tegh Bahadur, the ninth Guru.
every hymn in the Granth carries a raga in its heading
that heading is why some ragis hold to the raga.
Sikhs all agree on how Gurbani should be sung
some keep to the named raga; others sing simpler tunes so everyone can join.

games.q: you love the easy-tune kirtan everyone sings. your friend only sings in the named raga. before you argue, what's her best case?
o: the raga is named in the Guru's own book, so its mood is part of how the hymn was given.
easy tunes are disrespectful, and the Granth forbids every other tune by name.
ragas are harder to sing, and the harder way is always the holier way.
games.why: her strongest case comes from the page itself: the raga heading. your strongest case comes from the room: the sangat singing together. both love the same words.

practice: Listen for one sound near you that rises and falls: a fan, traffic, the fridge, your own breath. Follow it through the sit without naming it, the way a raga's mood moves under the words.
If you'd like, read all four hymns on ang 1352 first.
